battle.title: Isolation Gauntlet
battle.description: Dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads across isolation levels.

options: Reading data written by another transaction that has not yet committed
Reading the same row twice and getting different committed values
Seeing new rows appear in a repeated range query
Reading a row that was deleted long ago
questions.answer: Reading data written by another transaction that has not yet committed
questions.explanation: A dirty read sees uncommitted changes, which may later be rolled back. The second option describes a non-repeatable read and the third a phantom read.

questions.text: Within one transaction you read a row twice and get different values because another transaction committed an UPDATE in between. What is this anomaly called?
questions.explanation: A non-repeatable read means the same row returns different committed values within one transaction. A phantom read is about a repeated query returning a different set of rows, and a dirty read involves uncommitted data.

questions.text: Transaction T1 runs SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE status = 'open' and gets 5. Transaction T2 inserts a new open order and commits. T1 runs the same count again and gets 6. Which anomaly is this?
questions.explanation: A phantom read is when a repeated query over a predicate returns extra or missing rows because of another committed insert or delete. No existing row changed value and nothing uncommitted was seen, so it is not a non-repeatable or dirty read.

questions.text: acct(id, bal): (1, 100). Under READ COMMITTED on PostgreSQL or MySQL: T1 BEGIN; T1 SELECT bal -> 100. T2 UPDATE acct SET bal = 150 WHERE id = 1; T2 COMMIT. T1 runs SELECT bal again. What does the second SELECT return?
options: An error because the row changed
questions.explanation: READ COMMITTED takes a fresh view for each statement, so T1 sees T2's committed value 150, which is a non-repeatable read. Only REPEATABLE READ would keep returning 100.

questions.text: An audit job runs several queries and, by the SQL standard guarantees alone, must never see dirty, non-repeatable or phantom reads. Which is the weakest level that promises this?
questions.explanation: Per the standard, only SERIALIZABLE forbids all three anomalies. REPEATABLE READ is allowed to permit phantoms, even though some engines such as PostgreSQL go further and also prevent them.
